Pressure Mounts at Bessent’s Treasury Amid Staff Turnover and Unmet Goals
 
Plus, hear the radio commands enforcing the U.S. blockade of Iran, and meet the young Americans who moved to Israel after Oct. 7
 
 
BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Since he became Treasury secretary in early 2025, Scott Bessent has dressed down senior advisers and junior staffers alike over issues large and small, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former Treasury officials.

 

Yet President Trump has only pulled Bessent closer, pressing him to solve stubborn problems in the economy and end the war in Iran through sweeping sanctions. 

 

A senior administration official told our reporters the president’s entire economic policy agenda is on the Treasury secretary’s shoulders. “Scott cannot fail,” the official said.

 

His backers say his hard-charging style gets results. But 20 months into his tenure, Bessent is facing skepticism on Wall Street and an economy that could derail Republican chances in November’s midterm elections.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The FlyDubai attacker was part of a pilot hiring spree at the fast-growing airline.

 

• The “Cornell 7” lawsuit has reignited America’s debate over sexual consent.

 

• Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum is getting fed up with playing nice with the U.S.

 

• The U.S. has warned Moscow that its failure to disclose details about the death of a lab worker from a plague research center in Siberia runs counter to its international health obligations.

 

• As rancor over rising healthcare costs mounts, social media is brimming with content from influencers advising people not to pay high medical bills or sharing tips on how to cut them.

 

• A Chinese-born couple who paid a nationwide web of surrogates to bear close to two dozen children for them were arrested and charged with abuse on Tuesday.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Hear the radio commands enforcing the U.S. blockade of Iran.

 
 
 

No known tanker carrying Iranian crude has slipped past the U.S. blockade line since July, ship trackers say, cementing the effort as a highly effective blow to Tehran’s economy. Dozens of audio recordings reviewed by the Journal capture tense warnings, language barriers and confusion between the U.S. Navy and oil tankers’ crew members caught in the conflict. The audio recordings, shared by mariners in the region, illustrate how the blockade has been imposed and bring to life the experiences of civilian seafarers navigating the unprecedented geopolitical tension in the Middle East, report Rebecca Feng, Daniel Kiss and Jason French.

 

5.

 

Meet the young Americans who moved to Israel after Oct. 7.

 

A small, distinct population of American Jews has moved to Israel since the war, running against the tide of the many people leaving. Nearly 270,000 Israeli citizens left the country between 2023 and 2025, according to analysis by researchers at Tel Aviv University—the highest three-year emigration total on record. The figures run roughly 50% above the number of emigrants in the same time frame a decade ago, draining doctors, engineers and Ph.D.s in what Israeli lawmakers have called a “tsunami.” Countering that trend are young people who have spent the past three years doing the opposite: enlisting in the military, marrying and building lives inside a nation at war, reports Anvee Bhutani.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

In Idaho, a battle is under way for the future of the Republican Party.

 
 
Photo Illustration: WSJ/John McColgan
 

WSJ’s Robbie Gramer: Idaho, deeply Republican and mostly rural, is about the furthest you could get from a battleground state. So it is no surprise it is often overlooked in the national media during election cycles. But under the surface there is a groundswell of tensions between traditional Republicans, the MAGA loyalists and newer hard-right politicians tussling for power and influence in Idaho. This Mountain West state has become a key bellwether for the fight over what a post-Trump Republican Party could become at the national level, as well as a test lab for some of the nation’s most controversial conservative legislation. As a fourth-generation Idahoan, I pay attention to what’s going on in the home state. I recently returned to hear what residents think about the battle raging within the right.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

 

• The Fed releases minutes from its September meeting.

 

• Earnings: Levi Strauss

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$25 trillion
 

The estimated combined market cap of the Magnificent Seven at Tuesday’s close, a record high. Those gains propelled both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite to fresh records. Increasingly, the market is running on one engine: a familiar cast of tech companies that are building out (and benefiting from) the AI revolution. Just about everything else is going down.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Our travel columnist’s verdict on a robotaxi ride to the airport is in: It is relaxing, but really slow.

 

Ordering a predawn ride-share to the airport is always a gamble. You never know how long it will take to find a driver. Then you cross your fingers they won’t cancel. And there is always the risk of olfactory overload. None of those was an issue on travel columnist Dawn Gilbertson’s 5:30 a.m. Waymo ride to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in late September. But taking a robotaxi came with its own challenges.
